title: Tackling Size Generalization of Graph Neural Networks on Biological Data from a Spectral Perspective

problem.claim: Size-induced distribution shifts can impair GNN generalization to larger graphs.

gap.claim: Prior literature uses diverse assumptions about distribution shifts, while the spectral perspective on size-induced shifts has been largely underexplored.

contributions.claim: A data-driven approach identifies and characterizes size-induced distribution shifts and examines their impact on GNN performance from a spectral perspective.
In biological graphs, spectral differences driven by subgraph patterns such as average cycle length strongly correlate with GNN performance on larger unseen graphs.
Three model-agnostic strategies are proposed to increase GNN awareness of critical subgraph patterns, including size-intensive attention.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their data-driven, spectral-perspective analysis from prior work and describe the perspective as largely underexplored.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Across six GNN architectures and seven model-agnostic strategies on five datasets, size-intensive attention significantly improves graph classification on test graphs 2 to 10 times larger than training graphs.
The size-intensive attention strategy improves F1 scores by up to 8% over strong baselines.
The authors identify size-intensive attention as the most effective of the proposed strategies.

narrative_sequence.summary: The work addresses size-induced distribution shifts and their effect on GNN generalization to larger graphs.
Existing studies rely on diverse shift assumptions and reach varying generalization conclusions.
The authors use a data-driven spectral analysis of size-induced shifts, focusing on biological graphs with varied sizes.
Spectral differences associated with subgraph patterns strongly correlate with performance on larger unseen graphs.
The authors propose model-agnostic strategies and report that size-intensive attention improves classification on substantially larger test graphs.

source_observation.claim: Spectral differences driven by subgraph patterns strongly correlate with GNN performance on larger unseen biological graphs.

interpretation.claim: Subgraph-pattern-sensitive spectral structure may be a useful diagnostic for size generalization.

application.claim: When evaluating GNNs across graph sizes, inspect subgraph-pattern and spectral differences between training and target graphs.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that the relationship generalizes beyond the analyzed biological datasets.

source_observation.claim: Size-intensive attention was reported as the most effective among the proposed model-agnostic strategies and improved F1 scores by up to 8% over strong baselines.

interpretation.claim: Making critical subgraph patterns more salient may improve size generalization without requiring a specific GNN architecture.

application.claim: Consider model-agnostic attention mechanisms that emphasize size-critical subgraph patterns when test graphs are substantially larger than training graphs.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify which datasets, architectures, or conditions determine when the strategy is most effective.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the six GNN architectures, seven strategies, five datasets, or experimental protocols.
The abstract does not provide statistical uncertainty, per-dataset results, or implementation details.
